issues.legal_issue: A tenant that deliberately relies only on statutory protection from eviction cannot later raise an untried claim that the lease remained in force.
material_facts: The tenant told the trial court that it would not seek protection under the lease as to its term and relied on protection under the rent-control statute.
The issues and trial proceeded on that footing, and the tenant sought to raise the lease-continuance argument only in the appellate proceedings.
The lease had also ended by efflux of time after the suit was instituted.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not raise the lease-continuance argument at the appellate stage, and the appeal had to be decided on the footing that the lease had determined by forfeiture when the suit was instituted.
issues.legal_principle: A party that deliberately elects to confine its case to specified grounds and has the case tried on that footing cannot later introduce a different, untried basis for resisting relief. The Court applied this principle to the pleadings, counsel’s statement and issues framed; it cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.eviction_appeal_case: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree ordering a tenant’s eviction.
predicates.tenant_elected_statutory_protection_only: The tenant deliberately told the trial court that it relied only on statutory protection and would not rely on the lease term.
predicates.lease_continuance_issue_not_tried: The question whether the lease remained in force was not pleaded as an issue and was not tried before the tenant raised it on appeal.

issues.definition: When a tenant appeals an eviction decree after deliberately limiting the trial to statutory protection and leaving lease continuance untried, the tenant cannot raise lease continuance later.

issues.legal_issue: An occupier of a separate apartment is a tenant rather than a licensee when the grantor does not retain control and dominion over the apartment, and exclusive possession for valuable consideration can establish subletting when the tenant does not produce the grant documents.
material_facts: The occupants had exclusive possession of the rooms and paid monthly sums as consideration, although those sums were described as licence fees.
The tenant did not retain control or dominion over the rooms; the occupants could take away their keys, and the tenant’s control of the common corridor did not extend to the rooms.
The landlord produced evidence of exclusive possession for valuable consideration, while the tenant did not prove or produce the written agreements it said governed several of the occupations.
issues.conclusion: The occupants were tenants, not licensees, and the evidence supported the finding that the rooms had been sublet.
issues.legal_principle: The test for deciding whether an occupier of a separate apartment is a tenant or licensee is whether the grantor retains control over that apartment. Exclusive possession is an important, though not conclusive, indication of tenancy. The landlord bears the onus of proving subletting, but evidence of exclusive possession for valuable consideration discharges a prima facie burden; the tenant’s failure to produce the best evidence of the grants permits the court to infer subletting from the other evidence. The Court followed Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, [1960] 1 S.C.R. 368, and referred to Addiscombe Garden Estates Ltd. v. Crabbe, [1958] 1 Q.B. 513, Helman v. Horsham Assessment Committee, [1949] 2 K.B. 335, and Halsbury’s Laws of England, Vol. 23, Art. 1028.

rule.if: separate_apartment_occupancy_case and exclusive_possession and valuable_consideration and (grantor_retained_no_apartment_control or tenant_withheld_grant_documents)

predicates.separate_apartment_occupancy_case: The dispute concerns whether an occupier of a separate apartment holds as a tenant or as a licensee.
predicates.exclusive_possession: The occupier had exclusive possession of the apartment.
predicates.valuable_consideration: The occupier paid the grantor a valuable consideration for the occupation.
predicates.grantor_retained_no_apartment_control: The grantor did not retain control and dominion over the apartment, even if the grantor controlled common areas.
predicates.tenant_withheld_grant_documents: The tenant did not prove or produce the agreements that it said set out the terms of the occupations.

issues.definition: Where an occupier has exclusive possession of a separate apartment for valuable consideration, the absence of the grantor’s control or the tenant’s withholding of the grant documents supports treating the occupier as a tenant and finding subletting.

issues.legal_issue: A room’s exclusion from the statutory definition of premises does not prevent its subletting from being a ground for eviction of the tenant of the hotel building.
material_facts: The tenant held the hotel building, which was premises under the statute, and had sublet rooms within it.
The statutory definition of premises excluded a room in a hotel or lodging house.
The sublettings were found to have been made without the consent required by the applicable statutory grounds.
issues.conclusion: The subletting of the hotel rooms could ground eviction of the tenant of the hotel premises, even though a room in a hotel was excluded from the definition of premises.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(g) and 13(1), proviso clauses (b) and (c), of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, the hotel building may constitute premises even though an individual hotel room is excluded from the definition. That exclusion means that a sub-lessee of a hotel room cannot claim the Act’s tenant protection or seek standard-rent fixation on that basis; it does not mean the room is not part of the hotel premises or that its subletting cannot contravene the statutory eviction grounds. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R. N. Kapoor, [1960] 1 S.C.R. 368.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and hotel_building_is_tenant_premises and hotel_room_is_part_of_building and tenant_sublet_hotel_room_without_required_consent

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns a landlord’s claim to evict a tenant under a rent-control scheme.
predicates.hotel_building_is_tenant_premises: The tenant holds a hotel building that falls within the statutory category of premises.
predicates.hotel_room_is_part_of_building: The room that was sublet forms part of the hotel building held by the tenant.
predicates.tenant_sublet_hotel_room_without_require: The tenant sublet the hotel room without obtaining the consent required for the subletting.

issues.definition: If a tenant holds a hotel building as premises and sublets a room in that building without the required consent, the room’s exclusion from the statutory definition does not prevent the subletting from grounding eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A lease permitting operation of a first-class hotel and limited correspondence seeking regularisation do not establish the landlord’s implied consent to subletting where the lease expressly requires written consent.
material_facts: The lease expressly prohibited subletting the premises or any part of them without the landlord’s written consent and separately required the tenant to use the premises to run a first-class hotel.
The landlord’s letters to a government land officer asked that existing occupations be regularised and stated that first-class hotels commonly had airline counters and showrooms.
The correspondence concerned earlier occupations and did not amount to consent to later sublettings or to a general consent to subletting.
issues.conclusion: The lease and correspondence did not establish implied or general consent to the sublettings.
issues.legal_principle: An express requirement of written consent to subletting is not displaced by a separate obligation to operate a first-class hotel, because such a hotel can be operated without subletting. Correspondence requesting regularisation of particular existing occupations does not itself amount to written consent to those sublettings or establish general consent to later ones. The Court applied clauses 21 and 22 of the lease and the consent requirements in section 13(1), proviso clauses (b) and (c), of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952; it cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.subletting_consent_dispute_case: The dispute concerns whether the landlord consented to a tenant’s subletting.
predicates.lease_requires_written_consent: The lease expressly requires the landlord’s written consent before the tenant may sublet.
predicates.hotel_operation_does_not_require_sublett: The tenant can operate the hotel as required without subletting any part of it.
predicates.correspondence_only_requests_limited_reg: The landlord’s correspondence asks for regularisation of particular existing occupations rather than consenting generally to subletting.

issues.definition: Where the lease requires written consent, hotel operations do not require subletting, and the correspondence only seeks limited regularisation, implied or general consent is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord does not waive the right to seek eviction for unauthorised subletting without full knowledge of the right and the facts enabling effective enforcement.
material_facts: The landlord had visited the hotel and may have known of some occupants, but learned of other lettings only later.
The precise nature of the grants to the occupants had not been communicated to the landlord.
The landlord did not have full knowledge of all the sublettings and their terms.
issues.conclusion: The landlord had not waived the right to seek eviction on the grounds of unauthorised subletting.
issues.legal_principle: Waiver is the intentional relinquishment of a known right. It requires full knowledge both of the right and of the facts enabling the person to take effective action to enforce it. The Court applied section 13(1), proviso clauses (b) and (c), of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and relied on Dhanukdhari Singh v. Nathima Sahu, [1907] 11 C.W.N. 852.

predicates.alleged_subletting_waiver_case: The tenant claims that the landlord waived the right to seek eviction for subletting.
predicates.landlord_lacked_full_knowledge_of_right_: The landlord lacked full knowledge of the right or of facts about the subletting that would enable effective enforcement of that right.

issues.definition: When waiver is claimed in a subletting eviction dispute, a landlord who lacked full knowledge of the right or the facts needed to enforce it has not waived that right.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s unauthorised construction in breach of a known government lease condition establishes the statutory ground for eviction based on dealing with premises contrary to that condition.
material_facts: The government lease required prior written consent before a building could be erected on the land.
The tenant had notice of that condition and constructed an additional room without the required consent.
The additional room was let to an occupant.
issues.conclusion: The unauthorised construction established the ground for eviction under section 13(1), proviso clause (k).
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1), proviso clause (k), of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, permits recovery of possession where, notwithstanding previous notice, the tenant uses or deals with the premises contrary to a condition imposed on the landlord by the government when leasing the land. Notice of the government lease condition is sufficient notice for this purpose; the tenant’s unauthorised construction contravened that condition. The Court cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns a landlord’s claim to evict a tenant under a rent-control scheme.
predicates.tenant_knew_of_land_lease_condition: The tenant had notice that the landlord’s lease of the land imposed a condition requiring consent before construction.
predicates.tenant_constructed_without_required_cons: The tenant constructed a building or structure without obtaining the consent required by that land-lease condition.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a tenant who had notice of a land-lease construction condition and built without the required consent has dealt with the premises contrary to that condition.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not admit disputed documents as additional evidence when the tenant made no attempt to prove them at trial and the record does not justify a new trial.
material_facts: The tenant applied during the appeal to have documents admitted as additional evidence.
The landlord disputed the documents’ genuineness.
The tenant had made no attempt to prove the documents in the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The Court dismissed the application to receive the documents as additional evidence and found no ground for directing a new trial.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to reopen the evidentiary record where the documents’ genuineness was disputed, the party relying on them had not attempted to prove them below, and the circumstances supplied no ground for a new trial. The judgment cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this evidentiary ruling.

rule.if: eviction_appeal_case and appellate_additional_evidence_application and documents_not_proved_at_trial and document_genuineness_disputed and record_does_not_justify_new_trial

predicates.eviction_appeal_case: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree ordering a tenant’s eviction.
predicates.appellate_additional_evidence_applicatio: A party asks the appellate court to receive documents as additional evidence.
predicates.documents_not_proved_at_trial: The party relying on the documents made no attempt to prove them in the trial court.
predicates.document_genuineness_disputed: The opposing party disputes whether the documents are genuine.
predicates.record_does_not_justify_new_trial: The record supplies no ground for sending the case back for a new trial.

issues.definition: In an eviction appeal, a request to add disputed documents is denied when the requesting party did not prove them at trial and the record does not justify a new trial.
